issues.legal_issue: Only coal mining operations actually being carried on lawfully qualify for the statutory protection against acquisition.
material_facts: The purchaser claimed to have worked the colliery after acquiring it, but the High Court found against him on whether he had done so.
The colliery had been closed for years, and permission to reopen it was refused under the rule requiring prior written permission.
The purchaser nevertheless raised and dispatched coal, and later stated that he had stopped working the colliery in 1958; acquisition notifications were issued afterwards.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser’s activities did not qualify for the statutory protection because they were not lawful operations being carried on when the acquisition process began.
issues.legal_principle: The acquisition statute excluded from acquisition only land on which coal mining operations were actually being carried on in conformity with applicable enactments, rules or orders. The Court found that the claimed work did not meet that requirement because it was undertaken contrary to the applicable reopening and dispatch rules, and no operations were being carried on at the relevant time.

predicates.acquisition_exemption_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether ongoing mining work brings land within an exception to an acquisition power.
predicates.mine_not_operating_at_relevant_time: The mine was not being worked when the acquisition process reached the relevant stage.
predicates.mining_work_lacked_required_permission: The operator worked or dispatched coal without permission required for that work.

issues.definition: When an acquisition-exemption dispute concerns a mine that was not operating at the relevant time or was worked without required permission, the operations do not qualify for the exemption.

issues.legal_issue: Delay in deciding representations, without supporting evidence of bad faith, does not establish that acquisition notifications were issued mala fide.
material_facts: The purchaser alleged that the authorities had conspired to deprive him of the colliery, but the allegations were vague.
There was delay in disposing of his representations.
The Coal Board had previously declined to revise its refusal to permit reopening, and the record did not support a conspiracy between the Board and the Government.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition notifications were not vitiated by mala fides.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that delay by itself is hardly evidence of mala fides, particularly where the relevant authority had already declined to revise its decision. Vague allegations and unrelated personal hostility did not establish bad faith by the Government.

predicates.acquisition_notifications_challenged_as_: A person challenges acquisition notifications on the ground that they were issued in bad faith.
predicates.representations_delayed: The authorities took time to dispose of the person's representations.
predicates.no_supporting_evidence_of_collusion: The record contains no specific evidence that the relevant authorities colluded to bring about the acquisition.

issues.definition: When acquisition notifications are challenged as mala fide, delay in deciding representations without supporting evidence of collusion does not vitiate the notifications.

issues.legal_issue: A rule requiring prior permission to open or reopen a coal mine is within a rulemaking power directed to carrying out the purposes of coal conservation and mine safety.
material_facts: The challenged rule prohibited opening a coal mine or reopening one that had been closed for more than six months without prior written permission from the Coal Board.
The governing law empowered the Central Government to make rules to carry out the Act’s purposes and to take measures considered necessary or proper.
The Court found that the rule served coal conservation by allowing consideration of whether a mine should be opened and whether the country then required the grade of coal it would produce.
issues.conclusion: The rule was valid and authorized by the governing statute.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 17 of the Coal Mines (Conservation and Safety) Act, 1952, the Central Government could make rules to carry out the Act’s purposes; section 7 empowered it to take measures considered necessary or proper. The rule served the statutory purpose of coal conservation by enabling the Coal Board to assess need for a particular grade before permitting a mine to open or reopen. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.

predicates.rule_validity_challenge: A party challenges the validity of a rule governing the opening or reopening of a coal mine.
predicates.rulemaking_power_covers_act_purposes: The law empowers the government to make rules to carry out the purposes of the governing regulatory scheme.
predicates.permission_requirement_advances_coal_con: The rule allows the relevant authority to assess whether opening or reopening a mine is consistent with conserving coal and meeting demand.

issues.definition: When a challenged permission requirement falls within a rulemaking power directed to the scheme’s purposes and advances coal conservation, the requirement is authorized.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory power to regulate the grant of mining leases includes power to regulate their transfer.
material_facts: The purchaser acquired a colliery under a transfer that required prior governmental approval under the applicable Mineral Concession Rules.
The purchaser argued that the statutory reference to regulating the grant of leases did not extend to their transfer.
The Court treated mining leases as property and noted their typically long duration.
issues.conclusion: The word “grant” in the relevant statutory context included transfer of a mining lease, so the rules regulating transfers were within the rulemaking power.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that “grant” in section 5 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948, could connote transfer of property and was not confined to an initial grant. It distinguished Mason, Herring and Brooks v. Harris [1921] 1 K.B. 653 as involving a different context, and relied on Parliament’s express provision for rules governing transfers in section 13(1) and section 13(2)(i) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957.

predicates.statutory_scope_dispute: A dispute concerns whether authority to regulate the grant of mining leases extends to their transfer.
predicates.rulemaking_power_covers_mining_lease_gra: The law empowers the relevant authority to make rules regulating the grant of mining leases.
predicates.mining_leases_are_property: The interest transferred is a mining lease, which is property.

issues.definition: When a statutory-scope dispute concerns rulemaking authority over mining-lease grants, the fact that mining leases are property supports treating that authority as including transfer regulation.

issues.legal_issue: A person who acquired a mining lease in breach of valid transfer rules lacks sufficient interest to challenge the constitutional validity of a rule governing mine reopening.
material_facts: The purchaser acquired the colliery without the approvals required by the rules governing transfer of the lease.
The Court concluded that those transfer rules fell within the statutory rulemaking power.
The purchaser sought to challenge the constitutional validity of the mine-reopening rule, including under Article 19.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser had no sufficient interest in the property to raise the constitutional validity of the mine-reopening rule.
issues.legal_principle: Because the transfer rules were valid and the purchaser acquired the colliery in breach of them, he lacked sufficient interest in the property to challenge the constitutional validity of the Coal Mines (Conservation and Safety) Rules, 1954. The Court therefore did not entertain that challenge on its merits.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A person challenges the constitutional validity of a rule affecting the operation of a mine.
predicates.lease_acquired_in_violation_of_valid_tra: The person acquired the mining lease without complying with valid rules governing its transfer.

issues.definition: A person who challenges a rule’s constitutionality after acquiring the relevant lease in breach of valid transfer rules lacks sufficient interest to bring that challenge.

issues.legal_issue: Different decisions on permission to reopen mines do not establish unconstitutional discrimination when they were made at different times and the demand for the relevant coal grade could have changed.
material_facts: Permission to reopen the purchaser’s colliery was refused in 1957 because more coal of the relevant quality was not then required in the area.
Another colliery received permission to reopen in 1959, and its grade was fixed in 1963, five years after the purchaser’s grade had been withdrawn.
The Court considered that demand for the coal grade could differ after five years and that the later decision could be made on the facts then existing.
issues.conclusion: The difference in treatment did not establish discrimination in violation of Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not require identical outcomes where decisions are made on materially different facts at different times. The Coal Board could assess reopening and coal-grade questions on the circumstances and demand existing when it considered each case.

predicates.equal_protection_challenge: A person alleges unconstitutional discrimination based on different treatment in mine-reopening decisions.
predicates.mine_decisions_made_at_different_times: The relevant decisions about reopening or coal grade were made at different times.
predicates.coal_grade_demand_could_have_changed: Demand for the relevant grade of coal could have changed between the decisions.

issues.definition: When mine decisions are made at different times and demand for the relevant coal grade could have changed, the different treatment does not by itself amount to unconstitutional discrimination.
